02Personal project

Where should a driver go next?

A personal exploration of demand forecasting, reproducible ML pipelines, and serving predictions through an API.

Local historical-data demo

where_next

I’m building a forecasting system around a practical question: where might taxi pickup demand be when a driver is ready to reposition? The project connects historical NYC taxi records to zone-level predictions and a ranked heatmap API.

It brings together the parts of ML engineering I want to deepen: temporal and spatial features, baseline evaluation, model registration, incremental orchestration, and prediction serving.

LightGBMMLflowFastAPIAirflowPanderaDocker
01 / Forecasting

Beyond the obvious pattern.

Predict pickup volume per zone over the next two 15-minute buckets, using cyclical time features, eight lag offsets, and recent demand from five nearby zones.

Features & evaluation

LightGBM is evaluated against a last-week, same-hour baseline. WAPE lift and recall at top-K zones connect model evaluation to the positioning decision. MLflow tracks model parameters, metrics, and artifacts.

Weather, events, and supply-aware driver allocation remain future work. No driver revenue or idle-time improvement is claimed.

02 / Data & orchestration

Simulating a live prediction.

A Bronze → Silver → Gold pipeline handles schema validation, cleaning, and feature generation. An Airflow DAG advances historical data one 15-minute slice at a time.

Watermarks as simulation

The data watermark serves as "current time" for the simulation. The Airflow DAG simulates a live stream by replaying historical data in order.

The Airflow workflow reuse the same domain code, keeping the ML logic separate from orchestration.

03 / Serving

Predictions with context.

FastAPI exposes ranked zone predictions through /heatmap, freshness information through /health, and model provenance through /model-info.

API behavior

The heatmap endpoint returns zone identifiers, names, predicted pickup counts, and bucket times. Health information reports the simulated timeline position and publication lag, so consumers can interpret freshness.

The maps above are sample forecast visualizations from the repository. They illustrate API output from historical replay.

04 / Engineering practice

Make it reproducible.

Local Docker and Airflow definitions, configuration-driven features, and automated checks support repeatable development. The repository includes synthetic-data end-to-end tests.

Scope & next steps

NYC TLC records are published with a delay. The refresh cycle therefore replays historical data rather than consuming live taxi telemetry.

A closed-loop evaluation with simulated drivers, feedback-driven retraining, and personalized ranking remain roadmap items. Real-world driver outcomes have not been validated.

Personal project · Historical NYC TLC data · Local replay and API implementation. Forecast horizon and replay cadence are design settings, not measured business outcomes.
